claim: Tissue homeostasis is critically dependent on the function of tissue-resident lymphocytes, including lipid-reactive invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells.
source: Tissue homeostasis is critically dependent on the function of tissue-resident lymphocytes, including lipid-reactive invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about tissue-resident lymphocytes and iNKT cells.

claim: The T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire of iNKT cells from lymphoid tissues of mice and humans is highly diverse.
source: By analysing iNKT cells from lymphoid tissues of mice and humans we demonstrate that their T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire is highly diverse
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data and flow cytometry analyses presented in the manuscript showing diverse TCR usage.

claim: The TCR repertoire of iNKT cells is distinct for cells from various tissues.
source: By analysing iNKT cells from lymphoid tissues of mice and humans we demonstrate that their T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire is highly diverse and is distinct for cells from various tissues
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing different TCRVβ usage and TRBV gene frequencies across tissues.

claim: The distinct TCR repertoire of iNKT cells from various tissues results in differential lipid-antigen recognition.
source: By analysing iNKT cells from lymphoid tissues of mice and humans we demonstrate that their T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire is highly diverse and is distinct for cells from various tissues resulting in differential lipid-antigen recognition.
evidence: This is supported by tetramer binding experiments showing different binding capacities to lipid antigens across tissues.

claim: Within peripheral tissues, iNKT cell recent thymic emigrants exhibit a different TCR repertoire than mature cells.
source: Within peripheral tissues iNKT cell recent thymic emigrants exhibit a different TCR repertoire than mature cells
evidence: This is supported by data from Rag2GFP reporter mice showing different TCRVβ usage between GFP+ RTE and GFP- resident cells.

claim: The iNKT cell population is shaped after arrival to the periphery.
source: Within peripheral tissues iNKT cell recent thymic emigrants exhibit a different TCR repertoire than mature cells, suggesting that the iNKT population is shaped after arrival to the periphery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences between RTE and mature iNKT cells.

claim: iNKT cells from different organs show distinct basal activation.
source: Consistent with this, iNKT cells from different organs show distinct basal activation, proliferation and clonal expansion.
evidence: This is supported by data showing differential expression of activation markers like Nur77, ICOS, CD25, and CCR8 across tissues.

claim: iNKT cells from different organs show distinct proliferation.
source: Consistent with this, iNKT cells from different organs show distinct basal activation, proliferation and clonal expansion.
evidence: This is supported by Ki-67 expression and EdU incorporation data showing higher proliferation in LN iNKT cells.

claim: iNKT cells from different organs show distinct clonal expansion.
source: Consistent with this, iNKT cells from different organs show distinct basal activation, proliferation and clonal expansion.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data showing different CDR3β clonotype sizes across tissues.

claim: The iNKT cell TCR repertoire changes following immunisation.
source: Moreover, the iNKT cell TCR repertoire changes following immunisation and is shaped by age and environmental changes.
evidence: This is supported by data showing changes in TCRVβ usage after OCH and αGalCer administration.

claim: The iNKT cell TCR repertoire is shaped by age.
source: Moreover, the iNKT cell TCR repertoire changes following immunisation and is shaped by age and environmental changes.
evidence: This is supported by data comparing TCRVβ usage in mice of different ages (2, 6, and 11 weeks).

claim: The iNKT cell TCR repertoire is shaped by environmental changes.
source: Moreover, the iNKT cell TCR repertoire changes following immunisation and is shaped by age and environmental changes.
evidence: This is supported by data from antibiotic treatment and germ-free mice showing changes in TCRVβ usage.

claim: Post-thymic modification of the TCR-repertoire underpins the distinct antigen specificity for iNKT cells in peripheral tissues.
source: Thus, post-thymic modification of the TCR-repertoire underpins the distinct antigen specificity for iNKT cells in peripheral tissues
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including RTE vs mature cell comparisons and differential antigen binding.

claim: iNKT cells recognize self-lipids as well as lipids from pathogenic bacteria, commensals, fungi or pollens through their T cell receptors.
source: Accordingly, iNKT cells recognise through their T cell receptors (TCR) self-lipids as well as lipids from pathogenic bacteria, commensals, fungi or pollens; consequently contributing to anti-microbial, antitumor and autoimmune responses (Salio et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: iNKT cells contribute to anti-microbial, antitumor and autoimmune responses.
source: Accordingly, iNKT cells recognise through their T cell receptors (TCR) self-lipids as well as lipids from pathogenic bacteria, commensals, fungi or pollens; consequently contributing to anti-microbial, antitumor and autoimmune responses (Salio et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cells found in discrete tissues have distinct phenotypes and functions that critically modulate the outcome of immunity.
source: Beyond the common features shared by all iNKT cells (including their CD1-restriction and innate-like properties), cells found in discrete tissues have distinct phenotypes and functions that critically modulate the outcome of immunity (Crosby and Kronenberg, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Alterations in CD1d-lipid presentation in the gut or the liver result in dysregulated homeostasis of local iNKT cells driving increased susceptibility to inflammation in these tissues.
source: Consistent with this, alterations in CD1d-lipid presentation in the gut or the liver result in dysregulated homeostasis of local iNKT cells driving increased susceptibility to inflammation in these tissues (An et al., 2014; Zeissig et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Most iNKT cells express the canonical Vα14-Jα18 TCR α-chain in mice.
source: In mice, although most iNKT cells express the canonical Vα14-Jα18 TCR α-chain, they can use different Vβ chains
evidence: This is established knowledge about iNKT cells supported by the data in the manuscript.

claim: iNKT cells can use different Vβ chains.
source: In mice, although most iNKT cells express the canonical Vα14-Jα18 TCR α-chain, they can use different Vβ chains
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and RNAseq data showing diverse Vβ usage.

claim: The combination of Vβ-, Jβ-, and CDR3β-encoded residues will ultimately determine the type of ligands that iNKT cells can bind.
source: In mice, although most iNKT cells express the canonical Vα14-Jα18 TCR α-chain, they can use different Vβ chains and the combination of Vβ-, Jβ-, and CDR3β-encoded residues will ultimately determine the type of ligands that iNKT cells can bind (Cameron et al., 2015; Mallevaey et al., 2009; Matsuda et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A population of αGalCer-reactive NKT cells that express Vα10 TCR and has a distinct lipid-recognition capacity has been identified.
source: Moreover, a population of αGalCer-reactive NKT cells that express Vα10 TCR and has a distinct lipid-recognition capacity has been identified (Uldrich et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The majority of αGalCer-binding iNKT cells in humans express the prototypical Vα24Vβ11 TCR.
source: In humans, while the majority of αGalCer-binding iNKT cells express the prototypical Vα24Vβ11 TCR, populations of atypical NKT cells have been found in the blood
evidence: This is established knowledge about human iNKT cells.

claim: Populations of atypical NKT cells have been found in human blood, with cells expressing a range of TCRα and TCRβ chains that show differential recognition of lipid antigens.
source: In humans, while the majority of αGalCer-binding iNKT cells express the prototypical Vα24Vβ11 TCR, populations of atypical NKT cells have been found in the blood, with cells expressing a range of TCRα and TCRβ chains that show differential recognition of lipid antigens (Le Nours et al., 2016; Matulis et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The TCR repertoire of thymic and peripheral CD4+ T cells are not identical.
source: Accordingly, the TCR repertoire of thymic and peripheral CD4+ T cells (or that of recent thymic emigrants (RTE) and mature naïve T cells) are not identical, suggesting that certain clones are preferentially enriched and/or deleted in the periphery (Correia-Neves et al., 2001; Houston and Fink, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Certain clones are preferentially enriched and/or deleted in the periphery for CD4+ T cells.
source: Accordingly, the TCR repertoire of thymic and peripheral CD4+ T cells (or that of recent thymic emigrants (RTE) and mature naïve T cells) are not identical, suggesting that certain clones are preferentially enriched and/or deleted in the periphery (Correia-Neves et al., 2001; Houston and Fink, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference from previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The TCR repertoire of natural Tregs is unique for individual tissues.
source: Similarly, the TCR repertoire of natural Tregs is unique for individual tissues, is shaped by the local antigenic landscape and controls Treg-mediated tolerance to the tissues (Lathrop et al., 2011; Lathrop et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The TCR repertoire of natural Tregs is shaped by the local antigenic landscape.
source: Similarly, the TCR repertoire of natural Tregs is unique for individual tissues, is shaped by the local antigenic landscape and controls Treg-mediated tolerance to the tissues (Lathrop et al., 2011; Lathrop et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The TCR repertoire of natural Tregs controls Treg-mediated tolerance to the tissues.
source: Similarly, the TCR repertoire of natural Tregs is unique for individual tissues, is shaped by the local antigenic landscape and controls Treg-mediated tolerance to the tissues (Lathrop et al., 2011; Lathrop et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CCR7+ iNKT cell precursors emigrate from the thymus and home to peripheral tissues where they undergo further maturation.
source: In the case of iNKT cells, CCR7+ iNKT cell precursors are known to emigrate from the thymus and home to peripheral tissues where they undergo further maturation (Wang and Hogquist, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The percentage of iNKT cells using Vβ7 or Vβ8.1/8.2 chains varied according to anatomical location.
source: Within the iNKT cell population we found that the percentage of Vβ usage varied according to anatomical location, and particularly iNKT cells from LNs showed decreased percentage of cells using Vβ8.1/8.2 chains and increased percentages of cells using 'other' Vβs (other than Vβ7 or Vβ8.1/8.2) in comparison with cells from thymus or spleen
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: iNKT cells from LNs showed decreased percentage of cells using Vβ8.1/8.2 chains in comparison with cells from thymus or spleen.
source: Within the iNKT cell population we found that the percentage of Vβ usage varied according to anatomical location, and particularly iNKT cells from LNs showed decreased percentage of cells using Vβ8.1/8.2 chains and increased percentages of cells using 'other' Vβs (other than Vβ7 or Vβ8.1/8.2) in comparison with cells from thymus or spleen (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: iNKT cells from LNs showed increased percentages of cells using 'other' Vβs (other than Vβ7 or Vβ8.1/8.2) in comparison with cells from thymus or spleen.
source: Within the iNKT cell population we found that the percentage of Vβ usage varied according to anatomical location, and particularly iNKT cells from LNs showed decreased percentage of cells using Vβ8.1/8.2 chains and increased percentages of cells using 'other' Vβs (other than Vβ7 or Vβ8.1/8.2) in comparison with cells from thymus or spleen (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Significant differences in TCRVβ usage were observed for iNKT cells identified in non-lymphoid tissues including liver, lung and small intestinal lamina propria.
source: We also observed significant differences in TCRVβ usage for iNKT cells identified in non-lymphoid tissues including liver, lung and small intestinal lamina propria (SI-LP) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: After adoptive transfer, donor iNKT cells found in LNs showed a decreased frequency of TCRVβ8.1/8.2 usage in comparison with cells found in the spleen.
source: Interestingly, we detected the same shift in TCRVβ usage after iNKT cells (enriched from spleen and thymus) were adoptively transferred into congenic mice. Twelve days after transfer, donor cells found in LNs showed a decreased frequency of TCRVβ8.1/8.2 usage in comparison with cells found in the spleen, recapitulating the TCRVβ usage of endogenous iNKT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Adoptively transferred iNKT cells recapitulate the TCRVβ usage of endogenous iNKT cells in their new tissue location.
source: Twelve days after transfer, donor cells found in LNs showed a decreased frequency of TCRVβ8.1/8.2 usage in comparison with cells found in the spleen, recapitulating the TCRVβ usage of endogenous iNKT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The TCRβ repertoire of peripheral iNKT cells varies according to their anatomical location.
source: Thus, all together this data indicates that the TCRβ repertoire of peripheral iNKT cells varies according to their anatomical location.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments including flow cytometry, RNAseq, and adoptive transfer.

claim: The majority of TRAV sequences (>96%) identified in all of the tissues corresponded to the canonical TRAV11-TRAJ18 rearrangement (Vα14-Jα18).
source: As expected, the majority of TRAV sequences (>96%) identified in all of the tissues corresponded to the canonical TRAV11-TRAJ18 rearrangement (Vα14-Jα18) and showed highly conserved CDR3α sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: TRAV sequences showed highly conserved CDR3α sequences.
source: As expected, the majority of TRAV sequences (>96%) identified in all of the tissues corresponded to the canonical TRAV11-TRAJ18 rearrangement (Vα14-Jα18) and showed highly conserved CDR3α sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: TRB29 (Vβ7) and TRB13 (Vβ8) segments represented the majority of TCRβ usage in all the tissues.
source: In agreement with our flow-cytometry data TRB29 (Vβ7) and TRB13 (Vβ8) segments represented the majority of TCRβ usage in all the tissues and the percentage of usage for each gene differed between tissues (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1B-C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The percentage of usage for TRB29 (Vβ7) and TRB13 (Vβ8) differed between tissues.
source: In agreement with our flow-cytometry data TRB29 (Vβ7) and TRB13 (Vβ8) segments represented the majority of TCRβ usage in all the tissues and the percentage of usage for each gene differed between tissues (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1B-C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The percentage of the most abundant TRBV13-2 gene (Vβ8.2) was decreased in samples from LNs in comparison with spleen or thymus.
source: Specifically, the percentage of the most abundant TRBV13-2 gene (Vβ8.2) was decreased in samples from LNs in comparison with spleen or thymus and we also detected significant differences between tissues in the frequency of TRBV29 (Vβ7) and TRBV1 (Vβ2; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Significant differences between tissues were detected in the frequency of TRBV29 (Vβ7) and TRBV1 (Vβ2).
source: Specifically, the percentage of the most abundant TRBV13-2 gene (Vβ8.2) was decreased in samples from LNs in comparison with spleen or thymus and we also detected significant differences between tissues in the frequency of TRBV29 (Vβ7) and TRBV1 (Vβ2; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A highly diverse TRBJ usage and TRBV-TRBJ pairing was detected with notable differences for iNKT cells from individual tissues.
source: Moreover, we detected a highly diverse TRBJ usage and TRBV-TRBJ pairing with notable differences for iNKT cells from individual tissues (Figure 1C), which could suggest the existence of preferred TRBV-TRBJ pairing and/or the expansion (or deletion) of certain iNKT cell clones.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The CDR3β sequences were highly polyclonal without conserved motives or specific residues associated with individual tissues.
source: We found the CDR3β sequences to be highly polyclonal without conserved motives or specific residues associated with individual tissues (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Comparative analyses of length and physicochemical properties for CDR3β amino acid sequences did not find significant differences in sequences from iNKT cells isolated from various tissues.
source: Comparative analyses of length and physicochemical properties for CDR3β amino acid (aa) sequences (including hydrophobicity (based on the Kyte–Doolittle scale [Kyte and Doolittle, 1982]), isoelectric point (pI, according to EMBOSS [Rice et al., 2000]), frequency of polar (D, E, H, K, N, Q, R, S, T), aliphatic (A, I, L, V) or aromatic (F, H, W, Y) residues) did not find significant differences in sequences from iNKT cells isolated from various tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: A higher clonal size was detected for iNKT cells from iLN and mLN in comparison with splenic and thymic iNKT cells.
source: However, when we assessed the distribution of the iNKT cell TCR clonotype size (the proportion of CDR3β sequences which occur once, twice, etc. in a specific tissue), we detected a higher clonal size for iNKT cells from iLN and mLN in comparison with splenic and thymic iNKT cells (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: In spleen and thymus, CDR3β sequences appearing only once in the data-set represented around 65% of the total sequences.
source: Accordingly, while in spleen and thymus CDR3β sequences appearing only once in our data-set represented around 65% of the total sequences, this percentage decreases to 50% in mLN and 40% in iLN (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: In mLN, CDR3β sequences appearing only once in the data-set represented around 50% of the total sequences.
source: Accordingly, while in spleen and thymus CDR3β sequences appearing only once in our data-set represented around 65% of the total sequences, this percentage decreases to 50% in mLN and 40% in iLN (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: In iLN, CDR3β sequences appearing only once in the data-set represented around 40% of the total sequences.
source: Accordingly, while in spleen and thymus CDR3β sequences appearing only once in our data-set represented around 65% of the total sequences, this percentage decreases to 50% in mLN and 40% in iLN (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Cumulative frequency analyses provided evidence for increase in clone sizes in iLN and mLN TCR repertoires in comparison with iNKT cells from spleen or thymus.
source: We further assessed individual iNKT TCR repertoires for evidence of clonal expansion by using cumulative frequency curves to measure the 25 most prevalent clonotypes (Figure 1G). These analyses provided evidence for increase in clone sizes in iLN and mLN TCR repertoires in comparison with iNKT cells from spleen or thymus.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The TCRVβ repertoire and clonal expansion of iNKT cells varies according to their anatomical location.
source: Thus, all together this data demonstrates that the TCRVβ repertoire and clonal expansion of iNKT cells varies according to their anatomical location.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of RNAseq and flow cytometry data.

claim: The TCR repertoire of conventional T cells is shaped in peripheral lymphoid organs through differential modulation of the expansion and survival of individual T cells.
source: Once selected in the thymus, the TCR repertoire of conventional T cells is further shaped in peripheral lymphoid organs possibly through differential modulation of the expansion and survival of individual T cells (Correia-Neves et al., 2001; Houston and Fink, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In Rag2GFP reporter mice, GFP identifies RTE in peripheral tissues.
source: To identify iNKT RTE we took advantage of Rag2GFP reporter mice (Boursalian et al., 2004). In these animals GFP identifies RTE in peripheral tissues and the label is brightest in the youngest RTEs and decays over time until it can no longer be detected on T cells that have been in the periphery for more than 3 weeks (Boursalian et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work describing the Rag2GFP reporter system.

claim: In Rag2GFP reporter mice, the GFP label is brightest in the youngest RTEs and decays over time until it can no longer be detected on T cells that have been in the periphery for more than 3 weeks.
source: In these animals GFP identifies RTE in peripheral tissues and the label is brightest in the youngest RTEs and decays over time until it can no longer be detected on T cells that have been in the periphery for more than 3 weeks (Boursalian et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work describing the Rag2GFP reporter system.

claim: Small populations of GFP+ iNKT RTE were identified in all the analysed tissues of Rag2GFP reporter mice.
source: We identified small populations of GFP+ iNKT RTE in all the analysed tissues of Rag2GFP reporter mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the thymus, the majority of iNKT cells are mature tissue-resident cells (GFP-).
source: In the thymus the majority of iNKT cells are mature tissue-resident cells (GFP-) but there is a population of GFP+ iNKT cells that also includes cells in early developmental stages (Wang and Hogquist, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In the thymus, there is a population of GFP+ iNKT cells that also includes cells in early developmental stages.
source: In the thymus the majority of iNKT cells are mature tissue-resident cells (GFP-) but there is a population of GFP+ iNKT cells that also includes cells in early developmental stages (Wang and Hogquist, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GFP expression was higher in thymic iNKT RTE but comparable in RTE from spleen or LNs.
source: In agreement with this, GFP expression was higher in thymic iNKT RTE but comparable in RTE from spleen or LNs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The TCRVβ usage was different when comparing RTE and resident (GFP-) iNKT cells within the peripheral tissues of Rag2GFP animals.
source: We found that the TCRVβ usage was different when we compared RTE and resident (GFP-) iNKT cells within the peripheral tissues of Rag2GFP animals (Figure 2B) with a consistent increase in the percentage of TCRVβ7+ in the resident iNKT cell population compared to the recently arrived counterparts.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was a consistent increase in the percentage of TCRVβ7+ in the resident iNKT cell population compared to the recently arrived counterparts.
source: We found that the TCRVβ usage was different when we compared RTE and resident (GFP-) iNKT cells within the peripheral tissues of Rag2GFP animals (Figure 2B) with a consistent increase in the percentage of TCRVβ7+ in the resident iNKT cell population compared to the recently arrived counterparts.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CCR7+PD-1-Qa2low iNKT cells have been shown to emigrate from the thymus to the periphery where they terminally differentiate.
source: To further explore the peripheral shaping of the iNKT cell repertoire, we took advantage of a recently described strategy to identify iNKT cell precursors (CCR7+PD-1-Qa2low iNKT cells) which have been shown to emigrate from the thymus to the periphery where they terminally differentiate (Wang and Hogquist, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Populations of iNKT precursors were detected in thymus, spleen, and peripheral LNs using CCR7+PD-1-Qa2low markers.
source: Using this combination of markers, we detected populations of iNKT precursors in thymus and spleen (as previously described), but also in peripheral LNs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CCR7+PD1-Qa2low and Rag2GFP+ iNKT cell populations don't fully overlap.
source: Notably, CCR7+PD1-Qa2low and Rag2GFP+ iNKT cell populations don't fully overlap and while Rag2GFP+ NKT cells are enriched for CCR7+ cells, not all CCR7+ NKT cells are RTE (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) (Wang and Hogquist, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and a citation.

claim: Rag2GFP+ NKT cells are enriched for CCR7+ cells.
source: Notably, CCR7+PD1-Qa2low and Rag2GFP+ iNKT cell populations don't fully overlap and while Rag2GFP+ NKT cells are enriched for CCR7+ cells, not all CCR7+ NKT cells are RTE (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) (Wang and Hogquist, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and a citation.

claim: Not all CCR7+ NKT cells are RTE.
source: Notably, CCR7+PD1-Qa2low and Rag2GFP+ iNKT cell populations don't fully overlap and while Rag2GFP+ NKT cells are enriched for CCR7+ cells, not all CCR7+ NKT cells are RTE (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) (Wang and Hogquist, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and a citation.

claim: When comparing TCRVβ usage for CCR7+PD-1- iNKT cell precursors and 'mature' iNKT cells, consistent changes in Vβ usage were observed with an increase in the percentage of TCRVβ7+ cells in the mature iNKT cell population.
source: Nevertheless, when we compared the TCRVβ usage for CCR7+PD-1- iNKT cell precursors and 'mature' iNKT cells (excluded from the CCR7+PD-1- gate) we observed consistent changes in Vβ usage with an increase in the percentage of TCRVβ7+ cells in the mature iNKT cell population compared to the recently arrived counterparts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: After arrival to the tissues, iNKT cells are exposed to local signals that shape the newly arrived iNKT cell population into a mature iNKT cell pool with a distinct TCR repertoire.
source: Thus, these results suggest that after arrival to the tissues iNKT cells are exposed to local signals that shape the newly arrived iNKT cell population into a mature iNKT cell pool with a distinct TCR repertoire.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data comparing RTE and mature iNKT cells.

claim: Around 200-400 genes were differentially expressed amongst iNKT cells from various tissues.
source: Transcriptome analyses showed around 200–400 genes that were differentially expressed amongst iNKT cells from various tissues (e.g. mLN and splenic iNKT cells differed by ~200 genes; adjusted p value < 0.01, fold change >1.5) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: mLN and splenic iNKT cells differed by approximately 200 genes.
source: Transcriptome analyses showed around 200–400 genes that were differentially expressed amongst iNKT cells from various tissues (e.g. mLN and splenic iNKT cells differed by ~200 genes; adjusted p value < 0.01, fold change >1.5) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Compared to spleen iNKT cells, cells from thymus, iLN and mLN showed differential expression of transcripts encoding transcriptional regulators, nuclear factors, cytokine/chemokine receptors and molecules related to cytotoxicity.
source: Compared to spleen iNKT cells, cells from thymus, iLN and mLN showed differential expression of transcripts encoding transcriptional regulators (e.g. Fos, Fosb, Egr1, Egr3), nuclear factors (e.g. Na4r1, Tcf7), cytokine/chemokine receptors (e.g. Ccr8, Ccr4, Il12r2b) and molecules related to cytotoxicity (e.g. Gzma, Klrg1).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data.

claim: iNKT cells from iLN and mLN (but not from thymus) showed upregulation of genes related to T cell activation/TCR signalling.
source: Interestingly, iNKT cells from iLN and mLN (but not from thymus) showed upregulation of genes related to T cell activation/TCR signalling including Na4r1 (Nur77), Icos, Cd28, Fos, Fosb as well as the chemokine receptors Ccr4 and Ccr8 which are upregulated after TCR-mediated activation (D'Ambrosio et al., 1998; Sallusto et al., 1999) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3B and citations to previous work.

claim: Ccr4 and Ccr8 are upregulated after TCR-mediated activation.
source: Interestingly, iNKT cells from iLN and mLN (but not from thymus) showed upregulation of genes related to T cell activation/TCR signalling including Na4r1 (Nur77), Icos, Cd28, Fos, Fosb as well as the chemokine receptors Ccr4 and Ccr8 which are upregulated after TCR-mediated activation (D'Ambrosio et al., 1998; Sallusto et al., 1999) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Negative regulators of TCR signalling such as Dok2 or Ptpn22 were downregulated in LN cells vs iNKT cells from spleen or thymus.
source: Conversely, negative regulators of TCR signalling such as Dok2 or Ptpn22 were downregulated in LN cells vs iNKT cells from spleen or thymus (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Gene ontology enrichment analysis demonstrated significant enrichment in LN iNKT cells for genes encoding molecules related to positive regulation of T cell activation and positive regulation of cellular proliferation.
source: Indeed, gene ontology enrichment analysis comparing the transcriptome of LN iNKT cells with cells from spleen and thymus, demonstrated significant enrichment in LN iNKT cells for genes encoding molecules related to positive regulation of T cell activation and positive regulation of cellular proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The basal activation of iNKT cells is distinct for cells found in various lymphoid tissues.
source: Hence, these results suggest that the basal activation of iNKT cells is distinct for cells found in various lymphoid tissues.

Accordingly, iNKT cells expressing a variety of TCRVβ chains and CDR3β sequences generated in retrogenic or transnuclear mice were found to home efficiently in a variety of tissues irrespectively of their TCR specificity or Vβ usage (Clancy-Thompson et al., 2017; Cruz Tleugabulova et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The data supports a model in which local signals shape the TCR repertoire and specificity of the iNKT cell population after their arrival to the tissues.
source: Thus, while our data doesn't preclude that after thymic egress certain iNKT cell clones may preferentially home in specific tissues, it supports a model in which local signals shape the TCR repertoire and specificity of the iNKT cell population after their arrival to the tissues.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Tissue-specific programming has been described for various tissue-resident immune cell populations including macrophages, innate lymphoid cells or Tregs whose properties are controlled by local tissue-derived signals.
source: Tissue-specific programming has been described for various tissue-resident immune cell populations including macrophages, innate lymphoid cells or Tregs whose properties are controlled by local tissue-derived signals (Miragaia et al., 2019; Okabe and Medzhitov, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: While cells from spleen and liver display relatively similar transcriptional programs, adipose tissue iNKT cells present a distinct transcriptional profile associated with a unique (PLZF-independent) developmental pathway.
source: In the case of iNKT cells, previous studies have shown that while cells from spleen and liver display relatively similar transcriptional programs, adipose tissue iNKT cells present a distinct transcriptional profile associated with a unique (PLZF-independent) developmental pathway (Lynch et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The data shows a relatively similar transcriptome for iNKT cells isolated from thymus, spleen and LNs with only around 200–400 genes differentially expressed in these tissues.
source: Our data shows a relatively similar transcriptome for iNKT cells isolated from thymus, spleen and LNs with only around 200–400 genes differentially expressed in these tissues (in contrast to the thousands of genes differentially expressed by adipose vs. splenic iNKT cells Lynch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data and comparison to previous work.

claim: iNKT cells found in various lymphoid tissues likely share the same developmental program, but local signals in the tissues in which they reside shape their phenotype and functions.
source: This suggests that while iNKT cells found in various lymphoid tissues likely share the same developmental program, local signals in the tissues in which they reside shape their phenotype and functions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the transcriptome data.

claim: In the LNs, iNKT cells are recognising lipid antigens (e.g. endogenous or from commensals) that are not seen by iNKT cells residing in spleen or thymus in homeostatic conditions.
source: Accordingly, iNKT cells isolated from LNs show differential expression of genes related to T cell activation, TCR signalling and proliferation indicating that in the LNs iNKT cells are recognising lipid antigens (e.g. endogenous or from commensals) that are not seen by iNKT cells residing in spleen or thymus in homeostatic conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data.

claim: The catalogue of (endogenous and exogenous) lipids presented by CD1d in specific tissues could contribute to shape the population of iNKT cells resident in those tissues.
source: Thus, it is feasible to speculate that the catalogue of (endogenous and exogenous) lipids presented by CD1d in specific tissues could contribute to shape the population of iNKT cells resident in those tissues.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.

claim: Other signals (such as cytokines or hormones) likely contribute to modulate the phenotype and function of tissue-resident iNKT cells.
source: Added to this, it is likely that other signals (such as cytokines or hormones) also contribute to modulate the phenotype and function of tissue-resident iNKT cells (Holzapfel et al., 2014; Matsuda et al., 2002).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The observation that the iNKT cell TCR repertoire is shaped by anatomical location resembles the unique repertoire observed for natural Tregs which is also shaped by environmental antigens possibly controlling Treg-mediated tolerance to the specific tissue environment.
source: The observation that the iNKT cell TCR repertoire is shaped by anatomical location resembles the unique repertoire observed for natural Tregs which is also shaped by environmental antigens possibly controlling Treg-mediated tolerance to the specific tissue environment (Lathrop et al., 2011; Lathrop et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work on Tregs supported by citations.

source: The tight control of CD1d-dependent lipid presentation and peripheral iNKT cell homeostasis are also critical to prevent local inflammation.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge and the findings in the manuscript.
